community: Maiduguri (MMC and Jere), Borno State: Alau dam failure on the Ngadda River

C1.evidence: Official communication is in English. CLEAR Global notes English 'is spoken less frequently in rural areas and amongst people with lower education levels'. In the northeast, the 2019 MSNA found only 31% of people surveyed spoke Hausa as a first language, and Hausa and Kanuri were spoken by about 31% and 28% of households (CLEAR Global, via search summary). Even Hausa would miss most Kanuri speakers.

C2.evidence: ACRC: 'Poor residents settle on more affordable land along the flood plains of two rivers that drain the city. This land is only affordable because it is prone to flooding.'

C3.evidence: NiMet had predicted flooding (Wikipedia summary), and locals alerted officials to the rising dam. A state committee then reported 'there was no cause for alarm'. 'When the dam collapsed, actually no information came to the public' (Babakura Bukar, ACRC). The warning chain failed, not the forecast.

C4.evidence: The only channel named is officials giving 'interviews with the news media'. We found no cell broadcast in Nigeria, and Nigeria is not named among countries piloting it in the WMO/ITU 2025 EW4All update.

C5.evidence: Nigeria had 2022 floods (603-662 dead), 2024 floods (NEMA: 1,231 dead nationally, including Maiduguri), and the 2025 Mokwa flood (at least 151 dead).

C6.evidence: No source found that documents community radio or intermediaries as the trusted channel in Maiduguri.

warning_language: English (NiMet, NIHSA, NEMA). State messaging went through news-media interviews.
majority_l1: Kanuri and Hausa, among many others. English L1 is negligible.
l1_source: CLEAR Global language data for Nigeria (2019 MSNA northeast: 31% Hausa L1; Hausa about 31% and Kanuri about 28% of households): https://clearglobal.org/language-data-for-nigeria/

recent_floods.deaths: 30 (NEMA, early) to at least 150 (other reports); an ACRC interviewee cites about 77
1,231 (NEMA via Xinhua, May 2025); NEMA's DG cited 321 verified deaths in an April 2025 debrief (per search summary)

reforms: HEDA/NIHSA 2026 Annual Flood Outlook dissemination sessions are 'delivered in Hausa, Yoruba, Igbo, Pidgin, and English' (May 2026). NEMA distributes English and Igbo fliers. A blog claims that a 2025 decision to translate flood warnings into Hausa, Yoruba and Igbo was credited by NEMA with reducing displacement. That claim is UNSOURCED, so do not use it.
outcome_after_reform: unclear. No evaluation found. Kanuri is not among the listed translation languages.
notes: This is the closest analogue to a 'shared language would not have fixed it' case: the state explicitly said there was no cause for alarm. Language is a compounding factor on top of institutional failure. HEDA source: https://hedang.org/heda-nihsa-launch-nationwide-dissemination-training-and-sensitisation-on-2026-annual-flood-outlook-across-nigerias-six-geopolitical-zones/ . A HumAngle investigation of the dam failure exists but could not be fetched (HTTP 429): https://humanglemedia.com/maiduguri-floods-the-unfortunate-series-of-events-that-led-to-the-breakdown-of-alau-dam/

community: Lokoja and riverine Kogi State (Niger-Benue confluence); also Mokwa, Niger State

C1.evidence: The NIHSA Annual Flood Outlook and NEMA alerts are issued in English. CLEAR Global: English 'is spoken less frequently in rural areas'. The 2026 dissemination sessions add Hausa, Yoruba, Igbo and Pidgin, not the riverine languages.

C2.evidence: Residents in flood-prone areas did not relocate 'due to either disregard to the inherent dangers or inability to find alternative accommodation' (Leadership via AllAfrica, 2025).

C3.evidence: In 2022 NIHSA 'had issued warnings regarding imminent flooding in Adamawa, Taraba, Kogi...' states. In 2025 NiMet had warned of sudden flood risk in 15 states, including Niger State, before Mokwa. The Kogi household survey found 'access to flood sensitization resources from responsible agencies is poor', and only 68.8% of households had access to early warning.

C4.evidence: There is no cell broadcast. NEMA posts 'Flood Watch' on X. 'Household heads remain a major source of flood education' (Kogi study).

C5.evidence: 2022: 603 dead, with Kogi among the hardest hit. 2025: Mokwa flash flood, at least 151 dead.

C6.evidence: Community leaders and household heads were informal warning channels (Kogi study). The media 'plays a major role in translating and disseminating flood information to local communities' (HEDA, via search summary). There is no structured study on trust.

warning_language: English (NIHSA AFO, NiMet, NEMA); 2026 outreach sessions also in Hausa, Yoruba, Igbo and Pidgin
majority_l1: Kogi: Igala, Ebira, Okun-Yoruba, Nupe and others (no census L1 data). Nigeria has over 500 languages.
l1_source: CLEAR Global (no Kogi-level %): https://clearglobal.org/language-data-for-nigeria/ . No official language census exists in Nigeria. Kogi L1 shares are NOT sourced.

recent_floods.deaths: 603 (NEMA/Ministry of Humanitarian Affairs, reported by Tribune); NEMA's DG later cited 662
at least 151 bodies recovered; over 600 missing (CBS/AP)

reforms: Annual NIHSA Flood Outlook with community sensitisation. The 2026 multilingual dissemination sessions are HEDA/NIHSA.
notes: The minority riverine languages (Igala, Nupe, Ijaw, Tiv) are the gap. Only a blog asserts this, so treat it as a hypothesis to test, not a finding.

community: Nairobi informal settlements along the Nairobi, Mathare and Ngong rivers (Mathare, Mukuru, Kariobangi); Mai Mahiu / Old Kijabe, Nakuru

C1.evidence: PARTIAL. KMD advisories are in English. Nationally, English is the L1 of only about 3.5% of the population, and Swahili of about 27.5% (search summary citing Kenya census-based figures). In Nairobi, however, Swahili is the home language of 59.2% and English of 15.2% (Kenya Data & Stats, citing census data). Swahili messaging would reach most Nairobi residents, so the gap is smaller than in South Africa. For rural bulletins, NDMA 'bulletins are distributed to county governments in English' and volunteers translate them into Turkana.

C2.evidence: The flood impact was severe in Mathare, Mukuru and Kariobangi 'due to less solid structures, congestion, and poor sanitation infrastructure' (HRW). After the floods, riparian demolitions cleared up to 60 m from rivers (IDS).

C3.evidence: KMD 'gave more than five heavy rainfall advisories between 1 March and 15 May 2024'. The Auditor-General found the government 'failed to act on flood early warning information issued by' KMD and WRA. The public instruction was to 'relocate within 48 hours or be forcefully evicted', with no designated shelter.

C4.evidence: Cell broadcast is still at the roadmap stage. The Ministry is 'spearheading the rollout of a cell broadcast emergency alerting system using the Common Alerting Protocol (CAP)', with no deployment date given. A WMO 2025 update lists Kenya at the 'EW4All National Roadmap (2025-2027)' stage.

C5.evidence: The March-May 2024 long rains killed more than 200 by 7 May, and over 300 were later reported. The Mai Mahiu flash flood killed at least 50-61. Kenya also had the 2023 El Niño short-rains floods.

C6.evidence: Community leaders get KMD forecasts 'and translate them into languages commonly used locally, like Sheng' and Swahili' (PreventionWeb/Global Citizen). Youth volunteers translate NDMA bulletins for word of mouth and local radio (Context/TRF).

warning_language: English (KMD advisories); some Swahili via media and county channels
majority_l1: Nairobi home language: Swahili 59.2%, English 15.2%, Kikuyu 9.3%, Luhya 5.9%. National L1: Swahili about 27.5%, English about 3.5%.
l1_source: Kenya Data & Stats (census-derived) https://x.com/Stats_Kenya/status/1960956219151278222 ; Statista primary languages at home https://www.statista.com/statistics/1279540/primary-languages-spoken-at-home-in-kenya/ (national figures via search summary)

recent_floods.event: Mai Mahiu / Old Kijabe flash flood (culvert blockage under a railway embankment)

recent_floods.deaths: more than 200 by 7 May 2024; over 300 for the season

reforms: The Auditor-General's recommendations (DRM law, evacuation routes and centres), the EW4All roadmap 2025-2027, and the CAP cell broadcast rollout led by the Ministry of ICT.
notes: This is a partial analogue. C2-C6 match South Africa closely, but C1 is weaker in Nairobi because Swahili is the dominant urban vernacular. The strongest Kenyan C1 evidence is rural (Turkana): https://www.context.news/climate-risks/kenyan-youth-help-climate-hit-communities-prepare-for-disaster

community: Blantyre (Chilobwe, Soche hillside settlements) and Southern Region

C1.evidence: Chichewa is the dominant lingua franca. In the 2018 census, Chewa/Nyanja/Manganja people made up about 40% of the population, and large groups such as the Lomwe, Yao and Ngoni 'have adopted Chichewa as their native language'. DCCMS and the MRCS worked in Chichewa and English. Language is not the documented failure.

C2.evidence: The deaths were concentrated in unplanned hillside settlements such as Chilobwe (IJDRR 2025).

C3.evidence: The DCCMS alert went out on 7 March 2023. 'Weather forecasts focused on floods and not the movement of mud.' Residents 'said they were not told where to seek shelter, and so many stayed home' (Reuters).

C4.evidence: No evidence found of cell broadcast in Malawi. Warnings were 'sounded' through radio and officials, but many did not receive them.

C5.evidence: Cyclone Freddy 2023 left over 1,000 dead or missing. The 2026 floods killed 40+ across 29 councils.

C6.evidence: Communities with prior Anticipatory Action programming (Red Cross volunteers) 'were nearly 20% more likely to receive, trust, and act on early warnings'.

warning_language: English and Chichewa (DCCMS/DoDMA, MBC radio). The exact split is not documented in the sources.
majority_l1: Chichewa (dominant L1 and lingua franca); Lomwe, Yao, Tumbuka regionally
l1_source: Wikipedia, Languages of Malawi (2018 census ethnic shares): https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Languages_of_Malawi

recent_floods.deaths: over 1,000 dead or missing (presidential figure, April 2023)

reforms: Scaling of anticipatory action (MRCS). The sources recommend secondary-hazard (mudslide) forecasting.
notes: This is a partial counterexample on language: a shared majority language did not prevent the failure. The failures were hazard-type (mud, not floods), not knowing where to go, and poor reach. It shows that C1 is necessary but not sufficient to explain failure.

community: Beira, Buzi and the Pungwe/Buzi floodplains (Sofala); Chokwe and Gaza (Limpopo)

C1.evidence: 'Only half the population can speak Portuguese.' In Beira relocation sites, 41% 'do not understand written Portuguese'. Sena, Ndau and Chwabo 'are much better understood' (TWB/CLEAR Global, Idai 2019).

C2.evidence: 'Sudden flooding forcing people into trees and onto rooftops' on the Buzi/Pungwe floodplains (IASC RTE). Low-lying Matola, Marracuene, Boane and Manhiça flooded in 2026.

C3.evidence: In 2019 'the location of landfall and expected windspeeds were accurately known', but there was 'very limited warning about the floods'. 'Uptake and understanding of needed actions to take ... were less successful.'

C4.evidence: There is no cell broadcast. Mozambique 'updated its roadmap and built capacity on Common Alerting Protocol (CAP)' (EW4All 2025). Dissemination is by radio, megaphones and a 3-2-1 toll-free line.

C5.evidence: Idai 2019 killed 600+. Freddy 2023 killed fewer than 200. The 2025-26 floods had 43+ deaths in January 2026 and affected over 820,000 (INGD).

C6.evidence: 'Radio announcers convey early warning messages in local languages in each district.' After a Chokwe-Kendlemuka community radio announcement, about 500 people took early action (UNDRR).

warning_language: Portuguese (INAM/INGD). Since reform, also local languages via community radio and the 3-2-1 line (Portuguese, Changana, Macua).
majority_l1: Makhuwa, Changana (Tsonga), Sena, Ndau, Chwabo, Lomwe etc. Portuguese is spoken by about half.
l1_source: CLEAR Global crisis language map: https://clearglobal.org/mozambique-cyclone-idai-crisis-language-map/ ; TWB Beira survey (41% cannot read Portuguese)

recent_floods.deaths: at least 43 in January (INGD, via Copernicus/Wikipedia)

reforms: About 1,500 Local Risk Management Committees (CLGRC), local-language community radio, the 3-2-1 free line (Portuguese/Changana/Macua), and CAP capacity-building.
outcome_after_reform: Improved. Deaths fell from over 600 (Idai) to fewer than 200 (Freddy), and damages from US$3bn to US$500m (WMO). Hazard differences confound the comparison.
notes: This is the best African 'reform' analogue for South Africa: an official language that is not most people's L1, fixed by pairing it with local-language community radio and committees. It is the model for C1 plus C6.

community: Accra: Odaw basin (Kaneshie, Odawna, Adabraka, Circle, Old Fadama, Weija); Lower Volta downstream of Akosombo (Mepe, North/Central/South Tongu)

C1.evidence: English is the official warning language. Akan is 45.7% of the population by ethnicity (2021 census), and Ga, Ewe and others dominate locally. 'District radio stations' carry warnings 'with no national protocol governing warning content, format, frequency, language, or broadcast timing' (2026 study, via search summary). English L1 share is not quantified in the sources found.

C2.evidence: Accra has flooded in 2010, 2015, 2016, 2022, 2023, 2025 and 2026, 'with the same low-lying communities around the Odaw River, Alajo, Kaneshie, and Weija bearing the brunt each time'.

C3.evidence: 'The warnings are real. They are often accurate. And they are structurally ignored' (Modern Ghana). The World Bank-funded early warning system 'never went live... nobody in Accra got a warning worth acting on' (June 2026). At Akosombo, the VRA 'failed to give people a timely warning to evacuate'.

C4.evidence: Warnings go through 'radio, television, SMS, social media and community networks'. Ghana held an EW4All workshop but has no operational cell broadcast. NADMO launched an AI chatbot answering 'in several languages'.

C5.evidence: May 2025: 4-5 dead in Accra. 29 June 2026: 13 dead in Greater Accra. 2023 Akosombo spillage: over 31,000-35,857 displaced (no deaths in the Wikipedia article).

C6.evidence: District and FM radio carry warnings, and civil society led the Akosombo response (IMANI). No trust study found. The Akosombo response saw 'communication breakdowns and skepticism among community members regarding the information provided by authorities'.

warning_language: English (GMet, NADMO, VRA). Local-language broadcast is ad hoc, with no protocol.
majority_l1: Akan (Twi/Fante), Ewe, Ga-Dangme, Dagbani etc. Accra is Ga/Akan-dominant and the Lower Volta is Ewe.
l1_source: Wikipedia Demographics of Ghana (2021 census, Akan 45.7% ethnicity): https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Demographics_of_Ghana . L1 by language is not sourced.

recent_floods.deaths: no deaths reported in sources; 35,857 affected
13 (per YEN summary, rising from 9 to 12 to 13)

reforms: The GARID (World Bank, US$300m) early warning component was reportedly not live by June 2026. NADMO has a multilingual AI chatbot. There was a committee investigation of Akosombo (May 2025): https://editors.3news.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/05/Committee-Report_Akosombo-spillage-v7.1_May_7_2025_finalx-1.pdf
outcome_after_reform: No improvement evident. Accra deaths recurred in 2025 and 2026.
notes: This is a strong analogue on C2-C5 and on the 'no language protocol' point. Several Ghanaian news URLs returned 403 on fetch, so their quotes come from search-engine extracts. The Accra death counts are small compared with South Africa, but they recur.

community: Mt Elgon: Mbale City (Namatala and Nabuyonga rivers), Bulambuli, Bududa, Sironko, Namisindwa

C1.evidence: English (and Swahili) are official. UNMA forecasts are in English. The Bugisu population speaks Lumasaba/Lugisu (about 2.7 million native speakers). We found no source that UNMA translates alerts into Lumasaba.

C2.evidence: Landslides buried 125 homes across six villages on the Bulambuli slopes. The government has been resettling high-risk Elgon households since the 2010 Nametsi landslide, but 'progress has been slow'.

C3.evidence: UNMA's seasonal forecast placed 'highland areas in Elgon... on high alert over the risk of landslides and mudslides' (AllAfrica, March 2026). The Bulambuli CAO said locals had been 'sensitised' to keep off risky areas, but people had nowhere to go: resettlement was slow.

C4.evidence: Uganda is listed among EW4All implementing countries. No cell broadcast deployment found.

C5.evidence: Mbale, July 2022: 24+ dead. Bulambuli, November 2024: 22-36+ dead. Bulambuli, August 2025: 6 swept away.

C6.evidence: Elgon FM reported the disaster. No study on trusted channels found.

majority_l1: Lumasaba/Lugisu in Bugisu; Luganda nationally about 5.6m L1 speakers (2014)
l1_source: Wikipedia Masaba language (2.7m native speakers) https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masaba_language ; Wikipedia Luganda https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luganda . No regional % found.
reforms: The government allocated Shs 50bn to resettle over 5,000 households at Bunambutye.
notes: The C1 evidence is structural (official English versus a local L1) but not directly documented as a cause of failure. The binding constraint is C2/C3: people had no place to go.

community: Kinshasa: Ndjili, Kalamu and Makelele river valleys and erosion slopes (Mont-Ngafula, Ngaliema, Limete, Matete, Masina, Selembao)

C1.evidence: Mettelsat bulletins are in French. In Kinshasa 'French is spoken and understood by about 68.5% of the population' (CLEAR Global), so about a third are not reached in French, while Lingala is the city's vernacular.

C2.evidence: ACP (16 Jan 2026): 'l'occupation anarchique des zones à risque'; 'Plusieurs quartiers riverains des rivières et des collecteurs d'eaux pluviales sont régulièrement exposés'. In December 2022 'many of the deaths were caused by landslides'. In April 2025 most deaths came from collapsing walls.

C3.evidence: B-One TV (25 Sept 2026): 'Quelques jours avant, la MettelSat avait publié un bulletin annonçant des précipitations intenses sur la capitale. Mais qui l'a entendu ?... cette agence pourtant nationale est ignorée : peu relayée par les médias, peu suivie par les autorités, encore moins consultée par la population.' For April 2025, Actualite.cd's headline says Mettelsat 'avait déjà prévenu': https://actualite.cd/2025/04/06/pluies-et-inondations-kinshasa-la-mettelsat-avait-deja-prevenu-sur-des-phenomenes

C4.evidence: No cell broadcast found for DRC.

C5.evidence: December 2022: 169 dead. April 2025: at least 33 dead. November 2025: at least 2 dead.

C6.evidence: Radio Okapi is the main outlet, but no trust study found.

majority_l1: Lingala (Kinshasa vernacular); Kikongo/Kituba, Tshiluba, Swahili elsewhere. French is understood by about 68.5% in Kinshasa.
l1_source: CLEAR Global language data for DRC: https://clearglobal.org/language-data-for-the-democratic-republic-of-congo-drc/
reforms: Anti-erosion works before the rainy season (Radio Okapi, September 2026). No warning-system reform found.
notes: This is a very strong analogue: a colonial official language, a good-enough forecast that nobody listens to, and slope and riverbank settlement. The 'Mettelsat avait prévenu... mais qui l'écoute?' framing (B-One TV) mirrors South Africa's SAWS pattern: https://b-onetv.cd/inondations-a-kinshasa-la-mettelsat-avait-prevenu-mais-qui-lecoute/

community: Kalehe territory, South Kivu (Bushushu, Nyamukubi), on the Lake Kivu shore

C1.evidence: French is official and Swahili is the eastern lingua franca. No source found on what language, if any, warnings for Kalehe used.

C2.evidence: The villages sat where the Chibira/Chabondo and Nyamukubi rivers overflowed. The area had 'widescale and rapid deforestation' of the plateaux (ISS blog). It hosted 108,000 conflict IDPs.

C3.evidence: No documentation found of any forecast or warning issued for Kalehe before 4 May 2023.

C5.evidence: May 2023: 438 dead and 2,536 missing by 21 May (other tallies say 490). Bukavu floods in 2022.

majority_l1: Havu and other local languages; Swahili is the regional lingua franca (no % found)
l1_source: CLEAR Global, four national languages of DRC: https://clearglobal.org/four-national-languages-drc/ (no Kalehe-level %)
reforms: Reforestation proposals (ISS). No warning reform found.
notes: The deadliest event in this set after Derna, but we have almost no last-mile evidence. Treat it as a hazard analogue for C2/C5 only.

community: Chimanimani District (Ngangu township, Kopa growth point, Rusitu valley)

C1.evidence: Chimanimani residents speak Ndau. A search-engine summary states that after Idai officials found English 'could confuse rural residents' and later relayed messages in Shona, but we could not open the underlying source (pressreader, HTTP 403): https://www.pressreader.com/china/global-times/20210121/281522228743022 . This is unverified.

C2.evidence: 'Rivers and their tributaries burst their banks, and landslides washed entire houses away. The Kopa growth point area was particularly devastated' (MSF).

C3.evidence: 'The message about Cyclone Idai and how it was projected to affect Chimanimani did not effectively filter to the communities.' There was a 'lack of community engagement ... with respect to awareness-raising and evacuation drill exercises' (IJDRS 2021). Residents said 'Since there was a warning that the tropical cyclone was coming, we expected the Civil Protection Unit on the ground'.

C4.evidence: No evidence of cell broadcast. Channel details not verified.

C5.evidence: Idai 2019 killed more than 169 in the Chimanimani area (CPU). Cyclone Eloise hit in 2021 (MSD issued warnings).

C6.evidence: After Idai 'Zimbabweans pitch in and self-help' (TNH). Community self-organisation happened in response, not in warning.

recent_floods.deaths: more than 169 in the Chimanimani area (Civil Protection Unit, per IJDRS)

reforms: 'Learning from Cyclone Idai to strengthen Climate Information and Early Warning Services in Zimbabwe' (ReliefWeb). Content not verified (403).
notes: The documented failure is the district chain (DCP), not the forecast. The sources we could open do not confirm the language point.

community: Gofa Zone, South Ethiopia Region (Kencho Shacha Gozdi kebele, Geze Gofa woreda)

C1.evidence: The federal working language is Amharic (29.3% L1 nationally, 2007 census). Gofa is an Omotic language with about 360-392k speakers. No source found on the language of any warning reaching Gofa.

C2.evidence: Two landslides on steep farmed slopes. 'The second landslide buried those who had arrived to help in the wake of the first.'

C3.evidence: The National Meteorological Institute 'warned that unusually high amounts of rainfall would fall this year and could result in fatalities'. However, 'geohazards—such as landslides and earthquakes—remain a blind spot' (UNDP). Nobody told rescuers to stay off the slope after the first slide.

C4.evidence: Ethiopia is an EW4All implementing country. No cell broadcast found.

C5.evidence: The July 2024 Gofa landslides killed 257, 'the deadliest landslides in Ethiopian history'. UNDP: 2024 landslides 'claimed over 300 lives across the country'.

majority_l1: Gofa (Omotic) locally; nationally Oromo 33.8%, Amharic 29.3% (2007 census)
l1_source: Ethnologue Gofa https://www.ethnologue.com/language/gof/ ; national shares via search summary of the 2007 census

recent_floods.deaths: 257 (official); the UN warned it could reach 500

reforms: Impact-Based Multi-Hazard Early Warning Early Action System (IB-MH-EWEAS) Roadmap 2023-2030.
notes: This shows the 'warnings don't say what to do' failure (C3): the second-slide deaths came from people converging on the site. It is relevant to South Africa's KZN slope sites.

community: Beledweyne, Hiraan (Shabelle River); also Jowhar, Luuq, Doolow

C1.evidence: Somali is 'the first language of 93.7% of the population' (CLEAR Global / Ethnologue). SWALIM publishes flood bulletins in English and Somali, and its SMS system 'Digniin' is named from the Somali word for warning.

C2.evidence: Beledweyne sits on the Shabelle floodplain. In 2023 '85% of the Somali city of Beledweyne was submerged'.

C3.evidence: SWALIM warned of 'a flood event of a magnitude statistically likely only once in 100 years'. SoDMA ran awareness campaigns in Beledweyne telling people to clear waterways and stay away from vulnerable areas. The warnings were actionable.

C4.evidence: Digniin SMS alerts are pushed to at-risk communities, with radio broadcasts alongside (OCHA 2024 Gu update).

C5.evidence: The 2023 Deyr floods killed 110 nationally and displaced 1.1 million. The 2023 Gu floods killed 55.

C6.evidence: Designated community observers report flood incidents via Digniin, and warnings are relayed back through SMS and radio (FAO SWALIM).

warning_language: Somali (and English) via SMS, radio and bulletins
majority_l1: Somali 93.7% L1 (Northern Standard 60%, Maay 20%, Benadiri 18% per 2021 JMCNA)
l1_source: CLEAR Global language data for Somalia: https://clearglobal.org/language-data-for-somalia/ ; https://clearglobal.org/wp-content/uploads/2023/04/CLEAR-Global_Somalia-Hard-to-Reach-Areas-Assesment_-Language-Data-Analysis.pdf
reforms: FAO SWALIM EWS, Digniin SMS, radio, and bilingual bulletins.
outcome_after_reform: Improved. 'During the 2023 El Niño floods, more than 260 000 early warning messages helped evacuate 90 percent of the population at risk in Beledweyne' (FAO, 31 Aug 2026). About 250,000 people were evacuated to higher ground. 110 died nationally despite 1.1 million displaced.
notes: This is the STRONGEST counterexample. Warnings go out in the near-universal L1, pushed by SMS, with community observers. It was a 1-in-100-year flood, and the city was 85% submerged with a 90% evacuation. Caveat: the FAO figure is self-reported by the implementing agency. Source: https://www.fao.org/africa/news-stories/news-detail/from-data-to-decision--somalia-s-early-warning-systems-light-the-way-for-resilience-across-africa/en

community: Hanang District, Manyara (Katesh, Gendabi) on the slopes of Mt Hanang

C1.evidence: TMA issues 'tahadhari' (cautions) in Kiswahili. About 90% of Tanzanians speak Swahili (L1 or L2), though only about 15m of 47m speakers have it as L1. Local L1s in Hanang include Iraqw and Datooga (not sourced with %).

C2.evidence: Katesh town sits below Mt Hanang, and debris flows hit 'Katesh and Gendabi'. About 100 houses were destroyed.

C3.evidence: TMA's August 2023 seasonal forecast flagged El Niño rains. But IFRC: 'with the government not predicting and alerting communities in advance, there is a risk of people not engaging in response actions'. The landslide hazard specifically was not warned.

C4.evidence: Tanzania is at the stage of 'groundwork for nationwide Cell Broadcast systems' (EW4All August 2025) and held a GSMA/ITU CBS training in 2025. It was not operational in 2023.

C6.evidence: A 2026 study ('Beyond sensors and sirens: Community-embedded anticipatory knowledge systems...') examines local warning practices after Hanang. We could not fetch it (403).

majority_l1: Local languages (Iraqw, Datooga etc.) as L1. Swahili is near-universal as L1 or L2 (about 90%).
l1_source: Wikipedia Swahili (15m L1, 32m L2 in Tanzania; about 90% speak it): https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swahili
reforms: Cell broadcast groundwork (EW4All). President Samia ordered an in-depth probe of Hanang: https://allafrica.com/stories/202312080251.html
notes: This is a PARTIAL counterexample. The majority-language warning (Kiswahili) exists and is understood, yet 88 died, because the hazard (a debris flow) was not forecast or warned and no action instructions were given. Language parity alone does not prevent deaths when C3 fails.

community: Western and Northern Provinces (Rubavu/Sebeya river, Rutsiro, Nyabihu, Ngororero, Karongi)

C1.evidence: Kinyarwanda was spoken by 99.4% of the population in the 2002 census. Even so, the Red Cross pilot had to have Meteo Rwanda updates 'translated into the local language, Kinyarwanda'. This implies technical products were not in plain Kinyarwanda at the last mile.

C2.evidence: The Sebeya river burst its banks, and landslides buried homes on steep slopes. The government had 'previously asked residents living in wetlands and other dangerous areas to relocate'.

C3.evidence: On 2 May Meteo Rwanda predicted above-average rain for 10 days. The deaths came in an overnight event. A Karongi farmer said: 'Before, the rain came without warning.'

C4.evidence: Rwanda is an EW4All roadmap country. No cell broadcast found. The pilot uses SMS.

C5.evidence: May 2023: at least 135 dead in Rwanda.

C6.evidence: Post-2023 pilot: alerts shared 'through SMS messages, women's cooperatives, local radio, and even loudspeakers' by trained Red Cross volunteers.

warning_language: Kinyarwanda (plus English and French in official products)
l1_source: Wikipedia, Language policy in Rwanda (2002 census 99.4%): https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Language_policy_in_Rwanda
reforms: WHCA community-based EWS and anticipatory action pilot (Rwanda Red Cross, Meteo Rwanda, MINEMA) in Karongi.
outcome_after_reform: Improved in the pilot: 'During the last rainy season, fewer homes were damaged, and no lives were lost in the pilot zone' (Climate Centre, May 2026). This is small-scale and self-reported.
notes: Near-monolingual Rwanda still lost 135 in 2023, because of overnight timing and slope settlement. The improvement came from last-mile intermediaries (C6) plus plain-language translation, not from the national language alone.

community: Derna (Wadi Derna, below the Abu Mansour and Derna dams)

C1.evidence: Arabic is shared. The failure was contradictory content: the curfew imposed on 10 September overrode the mayor's 9 September evacuation order for five neighbourhoods. At 1:12 am the Ministry said the dams were 'in good condition'; they collapsed at about 2:40-2:50 am.

C2.evidence: The city is built along and at the mouth of the wadi, below two dams.

C3.evidence: The National Meteorological Center 'did issue early warnings', but they 'didn't address the risk posed by the ageing dams' (WMO). Forecasters warned 72 hours ahead (HRW).

C5.evidence: This was a single catastrophic event, not a documented recurring pattern at this scale.

reforms: The National Emergency and Crisis Management Centre was established, with calls for a multi-hazard EWS (WMO).
notes: This is a counterexample on C1 only. A shared language is useless when official messages conflict and a curfew keeps people home. For South Africa it shows that fixing language without fixing message coherence and 'what to do' will fail.

community: N'Djamena (Chari-Logone confluence; Walia and Toukra neighbourhoods)

C1.evidence: French and Modern Standard Arabic are official. Chadian Arabic is the lingua franca (40-60% fluent, about 12% L1). Pilots found 'poor translation of drought and flood forecasts into early warning' and that 'translating this concept [risk] into local languages is challenging' (UNDP/CREWS, via search summary).

C2.evidence: In 2022 'neighborhoods took on water and people fled the floods, with obsolete water piping and dike infrastructure no longer functioning' (World Bank).

C3.evidence: The humanitarian community launched anticipatory action for Chari river flooding in N'Djamena (OCHA).

C4.evidence: Chad is listed among EW4All implementers. No cell broadcast found.

C5.evidence: The 2024 floods killed 576 nationally, and there was a catastrophic 2022 flood.

C6.evidence: Local dissemination pilots at Linia, Maïlaou-Tchendjou and Bongor trained about 600 people (WMO/CREWS, via search summary).

majority_l1: Over 120 languages. Chadian Arabic is the lingua franca (about 12% L1, 40-60% fluent).

recent_floods.event: Chad national floods (Chari river at 8.18 m in N'Djamena)

reforms: PILIER (IDA): 250 km of drains cleaned, outfalls cleared, pumps installed, and anticipatory action.
outcome_after_reform: Improved in the capital. N'Djamena 'remained largely unharmed' in 2024 despite the Chari being 1 m higher than in 2022 (World Bank). This was an infrastructure fix, not a warning fix.
notes: This is a useful contrast: the gain came from structural and drainage measures, not from language or warning reforms.
